evals.prompt: I run devrel at Harbinger Labs. We maintain an open-source CLI for database schema migrations - Apache 2.0, no paid tier, no hosted version, and the founders have said publicly there will never be one. We're at about 11k GitHub stars and 60k monthly installs. The team keeps arguing about whether we should be aiming at indie developers or at enterprise platform teams. Can you settle it and tell me who we should be focused on next quarter?
evals.expected_output: A brainstorming pass that refuses the either/or framing, presents two or three whole candidate cuts of the same audience, deletes the buying-mode cut outright because no purchase exists, ranks the survivors out loud on effort/value/efficiency, recommends one, and stops before writing any segment map.
expectations: States it is in brainstorming mode and does not produce a finished segment map.
Presents two or three whole candidate cuts of the same audience, not variations of a single cut.
Explicitly removes the buying-mode cut from the candidate set because no purchase exists, rather than ranking it last.
Names that removal in writing rather than silently omitting the cut.
For each surviving candidate cut, lists the segments it produces, the artefact each segment would need, and who the cut makes unreachable.
For each surviving candidate cut, states what evidence must exist before anyone can be placed on one side of the line, and how much of that evidence the team already holds.
For each surviving candidate cut, states the condition under which that cut would be the wrong one.
Ranks the surviving candidates out loud on effort, value and efficiency rather than implying an order by list position.
Expresses effort as an order of magnitude of research work (hours, a week, a quarter) and never as a budget or currency figure.
Declines to answer "indie developers or enterprise platform teams" directly, on the grounds that the question presumes a cut nobody has chosen.
Recommends one candidate cut and leaves the decision to the person accountable before sizing anything.

evals.prompt: Quick one. I'm head of DX at Nimbus Relay - we sell a managed message-queue service, self-serve from $29/month up to enterprise contracts. Our roadmap for H1 locks in nine days and I need an audience decision before then so the SDK team knows what to build. Realistically I have maybe two afternoons to look at anything. What I do have: signup data with language and runtime on every row going back two years, and about 200 sales-call notes in the CRM. We've never run a user survey and we've never interviewed anyone about what they're actually building with it. Where should we land?
evals.expected_output: A candidate-cut pass that deletes the workload cut outright on the stated research ceiling and near date, keeps the ecosystem and buying-mode cuts because their evidence is already held, prices each at its real order of magnitude, and recommends exactly one.
expectations: Deletes the workload cut from the candidate set and says so explicitly, on the grounds that the research ceiling is hours rather than weeks.
States that a near decision date deletes any cut whose evidence the team does not already hold.
Does not propose user interviews or support-ticket coding as a prerequisite for the recommended cut.
Keeps the ecosystem cut available because language and runtime already sit on every signup row.
Keeps the buying-mode cut available because the sales-call notes already record who signed.
States that the ruled-out cut is deleted rather than parked at the bottom of the list, and gives the reason a parked cut gets re-proposed later.
Names which supplied constraint moved which candidate cut.
Estimates the ecosystem cut's effort as roughly an hour, given that language and runtime are already collected.
Estimates the buying-mode cut's effort as roughly an hour or two of reading sales notes and existing accounts.
Recommends exactly one cut for this horizon.
Does not present the default candidate ordering as a fixed rule.

evals.prompt: Context: Sablefish is a Kubernetes operator for stateful workloads. It only runs on Kubernetes - there's no VM build, no serverless flavour, nothing else planned. Last year marketing paid for a 4,100-response user survey and the agency delivered a clustering analysis on top of it; the clusters are sitting in a spreadsheet nobody has opened since. We're redoing our audience picture for the next two years - this is meant to be something we re-read and update, not a one-off. Which way should we cut the audience?
evals.expected_output: A re-ranked candidate set: the workload cut promoted to first because the survey and clustering already exist, the ecosystem cut dropped to last as non-discriminating for a single-ecosystem product, with the moves attributed to the supplied context and the existing clusters reused rather than new labels invented.
expectations: Promotes the workload cut to first place and names the existing survey and clustering dataset as the reason its effort collapses to near zero.
Drops the ecosystem cut to last and states that a product running only inside one ecosystem makes an ecosystem cut non-discriminating.
States that the default candidate ordering is a default rather than a law, and that it moves with what the team already holds.
Names which piece of supplied context moved which candidate cut.
Notes that a compounding, multi-horizon mandate favours the workload cut because it pays back over several horizons.
Does not recommend commissioning research the team already owns.
Recommends using the existing clusters rather than inventing segment labels first.
States the order in which attributes are selected, then clustered, and only then profiled and named.
Warns that a label invented first is usually a stereotype with no members behind it.
Recommends exactly one cut and leaves the final call to the accountable person before sizing.
Recommends storing the chosen dimensions, segment set, sizes and anti-segment so the next version can be diffed against this one.

evals.prompt: Board deck is Thursday. I need one number: how many developers are writing embedded firmware in Rust? I've got the RedMonk rankings open - Rust is sitting around 19th - and the last Octoverse report had something like 100 million accounts. Give me the figure and I'll drop it on the slide.
evals.expected_output: A sizing answer only: a range with method, date and confidence tier, a refusal to read a language ranking as a population or forge accounts as developers, a cross-check requirement against a different source class plus the company's own funnel, and a statement of what the number cannot support.
expectations: Returns a range rather than a single point figure.
States the method used to assemble the range.
States a date alongside the figure.
Labels the figure with a confidence tier of measured, estimated or inferred.
Refuses to read the RedMonk rank as a population count or as a market share.
States that RedMonk's own publisher treats the tier as more meaningful than the individual rank.
Refuses to treat forge account counts as a count of professional developers, naming bots, duplicates or dormant accounts as inflation.
States what the number cannot support, not only what it can.
Requires a cross-check against a source of a different class, and states that two sources of the same class usually share an upstream dataset.
Recommends a bottom-up cross-check against the company's own funnel.
Does not produce a full segment map, segment scoring or a primary-segment recommendation.

evals.prompt: We've been going back and forth on this for a month so I'm just going to decide. Kettlewell is a CI runner product; we're Node-and-Python-first and always have been. Java is 1.9% of our signups and 2.3% of active workspaces. Someone keeps pushing to build a Maven plugin and a Java quickstart for 'the JVM enterprise segment'. 1.9% is 1.9% - that segment is tiny and I want to close this out. Back me up?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to size an unserved segment from first-party data, an external estimate shaped with range/method/date/confidence, and a cheap falsifiable test with its drop condition written before it runs.
expectations: Refuses to accept the 1.9% signup share as evidence that the JVM segment is small.
States that first-party data is survivorship-shaped and describes only who already got through the funnel.
States that sizing an unserved segment from your own user base returns "small" by construction.
Proposes an external estimate of the JVM population built from a source outside the company's own funnel.
Requires that estimate to carry a range, a method, a date and a confidence tier.
Notes that the product being Node-and-Python-first is itself a plausible cause of the low Java share.
Proposes a cheap test that could settle the question in days rather than a quarter.
States the result that would make the team genuinely drop the segment, written before the test runs.
Does not endorse killing the segment on the strength of the funnel number alone.
Treats the segment as a hypothesis segment rather than a confirmed small one while its evidence sits below the floor.

evals.prompt: Sizing exercise for Loomstack - we make an evaluation harness for LLM applications. Here's what I pulled: 2.1 million models published on the big open model hub, 940,000 datasets, and our own package has 380,000 downloads a month on the language registry. I make that a very large addressable segment of ML engineers. Sanity-check my maths and give me the segment size.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of catalogue size and registry downloads as market size, with the download-concentration evidence quoted, a statement of what hub data legitimately supports, and a properly shaped range with method, date, confidence tier and a different-class cross-check.
expectations: Refuses to treat the hub's catalogue size as a market size.
States that publishing on these hubs is free and unreviewed, so the counts measure publishing activity.
Cites the finding that the large majority of published models have fewer than a couple of hundred lifetime downloads.
Cites that a tiny fraction of repositories accounts for almost all downloads on such a hub.
States that "millions of models exist" and "millions of models are used" differ by roughly two orders of magnitude.
Refuses to treat package-registry downloads as human users, naming CI re-downloads as a dominant contributor.
States what hub and registry data can legitimately support: the shape of the practitioner niche, such as which tasks, formats or base models the segment works with.
Returns a range with a method, a date and a confidence tier rather than a single figure.
Requires a cross-check against a source of a different class.
Labels any figure with no data behind it as inferred and names the lookup that would upgrade it.

evals.prompt: I'm at Tarnhelm Insurance. We've published a claims API and a set of webhooks so brokers' engineering teams can integrate with us directly - it's one of about six channels we sell through, and the API isn't sold separately, it comes with the broker contract. Our devrel person keeps saying we need better quickstarts and a nicer sandbox. Meanwhile two integrations this year died somewhere after the technical proof of concept. I've got notes from four deals that closed and three that didn't. Who are we actually segmenting here?
evals.expected_output: A decision-unit pass: the company classified as developer-plus, evaluator/champion/approver/buyer named per segment, the post-POC deaths traced to an approver role, a segment split where the decision unit differs, and the questions aimed at the recorded wins and losses.
expectations: Classifies the company as developer-plus rather than developer-first, and gives the reason.
Names, for each segment, who evaluates, who approves and who signs.
Identifies an approver role (architect, platform lead, security or legal reviewer) as the likely cause of integrations dying after the technical proof of concept.
States that one unanswered risk question is enough for an approver to say no.
Identifies champion material as the highest-leverage artefact in company adoption, because the champion argues when nobody from the vendor is in the room.
Splits a nominal segment into two when its decision unit differs, rather than recording the difference as a footnote.
Names a concrete trigger that adds an approver, such as a regulated vertical or a company-size threshold.
Directs its diagnostic questions at the recorded recent wins and recent losses rather than at an abstract org chart.
Asks which role blocked each loss and what would have unblocked them.
Warns that developer-delight material alone loses at the security or risk review.
Names which artefacts serve both adoption paths so they get built once.

evals.prompt: Byrnewood Analytics, embedded charting library. Paid SDK licence, $1,200 per seat per year, sold to product teams. But our single biggest audience by volume is university students and bootcamp people using the free educational licence - something like 40,000 of them against 900 paying seats. Marketing wants to make students a headline segment in the new audience plan because the numbers look great. Draft the segment rows.
evals.expected_output: Segment rows in which the free student audience must be justified against a named non-revenue driver or moved to the anti-segment, with raw volume rejected as a reason, and every row carrying a sized range, a decision unit and differentiated artefact/channel/proof.
expectations: Requires the student segment to be justified against a named non-revenue driver before it can be funded.
Names the available non-revenue drivers explicitly: talent brand, contributor supply, future buyers, or ecosystem gravity.
States that without one of those written down, the segment belongs in the anti-segment.
Warns that an unjustified free audience quietly absorbs content and support capacity precisely because it is the easiest to reach.
Rejects raw volume on its own as a reason to make the segment a headline.
Notes that the future-buyers justification operates on a horizon measured in years rather than quarters.
Records the student segment's decision unit as "no purchase exists" rather than inventing a buyer for it.
Keeps the map to three to five segments.
Gives every segment row a size expressed as a range with a method, a date and a confidence tier.
Gives every segment row an artefact, a channel and a proof point that differ from at least one sibling row.

evals.prompt: Here's our segment scorecard for Vantablack Systems - we do hardware-in-the-loop test infrastructure, funded this year explicitly to help sales close bigger deals. I scored each segment out of 10 on size, reach, fit, value, effort, competition and compounding, then summed the seven. Independent hardware hobbyists came out top on 61/70 because they're huge, easy to reach and cost us nothing. Automotive tier-one suppliers came out bottom on 44/70, mostly because effort scored 3. So: hobbyists primary. Write it up.
evals.expected_output: A rebuilt ranking: coarse scale, criteria weighted against the sales-enablement driver before scoring, effort divided out rather than summed in, the division shown, the starved high-value/high-effort segment named with its promotion conditions, and a committed primary/secondary/anti shape.
expectations: Rejects summing effort into the total, and states that effort is the denominator rather than another addend.
Rejects the 1-10 scale and replaces it with a 1-3 or high/medium/low scale.
Gives the reason for the coarse scale: false precision moves the argument onto the score instead of onto the segment.
Weights the criteria against the funded driver before scoring, not after.
Names sales enablement as the funded driver here and weights value and competitive position accordingly.
Notes that a segment carrying no revenue value is a defect under a sales-enablement driver even though it would be acceptable under an employer-brand driver.
Re-ranks by value per unit of effort and shows the division explicitly.
States which segment lost on the denominator rather than on merit.
Names what the efficiency ratio starves: the big, high-value, high-effort segment that loses every round it is ranked in.
Names the conditions that promote the starved segment anyway, including a sales-enablement driver with no cheaper segment carrying revenue.
Does not leave the hobbyist segment as primary without testing it against the funded driver.
Commits to exactly one primary segment, one secondary and one anti-segment.

evals.prompt: Final read before I send this to the exec team. Product is Quillfold, a headless CMS with an API-first pitch. We've landed on three segments: agency developers building client sites, in-house product teams at mid-market SaaS companies, and marketing-ops people who write a bit of code. Primary is in-house product teams. Secondary is agency developers - we've budgeted a dedicated agency partner portal, an agency-specific webinar series and a separate docs track for them. Plan for next quarter: ship the partner portal, publish the migration guides, do the four webinars, and keep the weekly newsletter going. Anything missing?
evals.expected_output: A gate check that fails the map on a missing anti-segment, a secondary funded with its own dedicated artefacts, implications with no stop, missing sizes and decision units, and no review date or early re-read triggers.
expectations: Flags the absence of an anti-segment as a gate failure.
Requires the anti-segment to be non-empty and to include at least one audience the team wanted to keep.
Rejects the secondary segment having its own dedicated artefacts, and restates that a secondary is served only by artefacts the primary already funds.
Names the partner portal, the agency webinar series and the agency docs track as the dedicated spend that breaks that rule.
Requires the implications section to name something that stops, not only things that start.
Flags the absence of a review date.

Names concrete events that would force an early re-read, such as a pricing or packaging change, a new language or runtime target, a change in the funded driver, a competitor taking the primary segment's default position, or the primary segment hitting its goal.
Flags that every segment needs a size with a range, a method, a date and a confidence tier, none of which are present.
Flags that every segment needs a named decision unit, or an explicit statement that no purchase exists.
Checks that each segment is described in language its own members would recognise rather than in internal category names.
Reports the gate check explicitly rather than implying the map passed.

evals.prompt: We want to fund a whole new SDK next quarter for what we're calling 'air-gapped defence integrators' - Ravenhollow Data, we do log pipeline tooling. Honest state of the evidence: one lost deal where the guy mentioned it, and one conversation at a conference booth. Everyone on the team is convinced it's real and the SDK is about four engineer-months. Put it in the plan as a funded segment.
evals.expected_output: The segment kept in the map but labelled a hypothesis and left unfunded until it clears the evidence floor, with a days-long falsifiable test, its drop condition written in advance, and the funding request refused on the current two data points.
expectations: Labels the air-gapped defence integrators segment a hypothesis segment.
States the evidence floor as roughly 5-10 independent data points from a consistent group.
States that the floor is a customer-research practice convention rather than a measured threshold.
Keeps the segment in the map rather than deleting it.
Leaves the segment unfunded until it clears the floor.
Refuses to commit the four engineer-months of SDK work on the current evidence.
Names a specific cheap test that costs days rather than a quarter.
States the result that would make the team drop the segment, written before the test runs.
Requires at least half the funded segments in the map to clear the evidence floor.
Does not present the two data points as measured evidence.
Names which lookup or source would upgrade the segment's size from inferred.

evals.prompt: Inherited this from the person who had my job before me. Company is Windrose Telemetry. Our audience doc has three personas: 'Junior Jamie', a bootcamp grad in their first year who loves learning; 'Mid-level Morgan', three to six years in, pragmatic, time-poor; and 'Staff-level Sam', ten years in, opinionated, hates marketing. Each has a page of day-in-the-life narrative. Size is listed as 'Large', '~4 million' and 'Growing'. Next steps at the bottom say: more content for Morgan, plus a beginner tutorial series. Tidy this up for me and make it presentable.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the seniority cut rather than a tidy-up, with the two conditions under which seniority earns a place, the prose-portrait format refused, the unsourced sizes refused, the contradiction between ranking and next steps flagged, and a replacement two-dimension cut proposed.
expectations: Rejects seniority as the axis of the cut rather than tidying the existing personas.
States that a junior and a staff engineer on the same stack and workload usually need the same SDK, docs and samples.
Names the only two conditions under which seniority earns a place: when it maps onto authority, or onto learning need.
Records seniority as a descriptive field inside a segment when it does not clear those conditions.
Rejects the day-in-the-life narrative format, stating that a prose portrait reads well and decides nothing.
States that a persona averaged across segments represents nobody.
Rejects "Large", "~4 million" and "Growing" as sizes carrying no source, date, method or confidence tier.
Flags that the "~4 million" figure is most likely a language ranking or an account count read as a population.
Flags that the next steps contradict the ranking, because a beginner tutorial series serves the segment the doc deprioritised.
States that two segments receiving identical artefacts are one segment with a demographic footnote, and that the dimension was therefore wrong.
Proposes a replacement cut with exactly two dimensions, one that changes what gets built and one that changes how they are reached.

evals.prompt: Dredgewater Compute. We did a developer segment map last September - I've still got the doc, it named mid-size gaming studios primary, indie game developers secondary, and put VFX and animation houses in the anti-segment because we couldn't do the colour-pipeline work. Twelve months on, someone wants me to redo the whole exercise from scratch. We shipped two things for gaming studios and one general 'for developers' performance guide. Studio share of new signups went from 18% to 31%. What should I actually do here?
evals.expected_output: A re-read of the stored map returning a diff rather than a rebuild: what moved, which predictions held, which segments to retire, the concentration and artefact-fit readings on the shipped work, and a new review date with early re-read triggers.
expectations: Runs a re-read against the stored map rather than rebuilding it from a blank page.
Returns a diff: what moved, which predictions held, and which segments to retire.
Reads the studio signup share moving from 18% to 31% as the concentration measure improving.
Counts the general "for developers" performance guide as an artefact-fit miss, because it was not built for a named segment.
Checks prediction accuracy by asking which sized segments actually behaved as the map predicted.
States that a wrong prediction should correct the sizing method rather than the conclusion.
Includes argument frequency - how often the team reopens the audience question - as a measure of whether the map worked.
Re-checks whether the anti-segment's stated reason still holds before retiring or keeping that exclusion.
Names the events that would force an early re-read before the next scheduled review.
Sets a new review date on the updated map.
